title: (Scenario) EC2 instances fail ALB health checks / an RDS runs out of storage / a production deployment fails — walk through your immediate mitigation and your longer-term fix.
shortTitle: Immediate mitigation and longer-term fix for EC2 ALB health-check failures, RDS storage exhaustion, and failed production deployments

s1_definition.profdef: For each failure you separate immediate mitigation — the fastest safe action to restore service — from the longer-term fix that prevents recurrence. For EC2 instances failing ALB health checks, you remove or replace the bad instances and let auto-scaling bring healthy capacity, then fix the probe or startup issue. For an RDS running out of storage, you grow storage immediately (or enable storage autoscaling) then address the growth driver. For a failed production deployment, you roll back to the last known-good version immediately, then fix the pipeline gap that let the bad build through.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, three different emergencies need two kinds of response each. If some teller counters stop responding (EC2 failing health checks), you first close those counters and open fresh ones (replace instances), then investigate why they froze. If the vault's ledger storage is almost full (RDS out of storage), you first add more shelves immediately (grow storage), then find out why paperwork is piling up. If you rolled out a new process that broke everything (failed deployment), you first revert to yesterday's working process (rollback), then fix the approval checks that let the broken process ship.
s1_definition.oneliner: Always mitigate first to stop the bleeding — replace unhealthy instances, grow storage, roll back the deploy — and only then do the longer-term fix that prevents it happening again.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** For each failure you separate immediate mitigation — the fastest safe action to restore service — from the longer-term fix that prevents recurrence. For EC2 instances failing ALB health checks, you remove or replace the bad instances and let auto-scaling bring healthy capacity, then fix the probe or startup issue. For an RDS running out of storage, you grow storage immediately (or enable storage autoscaling) then address the growth driver. For a failed production deployment, you roll back to the last known-good version immediately, then fix the pipeline gap that let the bad build through.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, three different emergencies need two kinds of response each. If some teller counters stop responding (EC2 failing health checks), you first close those counters and open fresh ones (replace instances), then investigate why they froze. If the vault's ledger storage is almost full (RDS out of storage), you first add more shelves immediately (grow storage), then find out why paperwork is piling up. If you rolled out a new process that broke everything (failed deployment), you first revert to yesterday's working process (rollback), then fix the approval checks that let the broken process ship.

**One line to remember:** Always mitigate first to stop the bleeding — replace unhealthy instances, grow storage, roll back the deploy — and only then do the longer-term fix that prevents it happening again.

sections.s2_technical:
For EC2 instances failing ALB health checks, the immediate mitigation is to stop sending traffic to the unhealthy instances. The ALB already does this by marking them unhealthy and routing around them, so your job is to ensure the Auto Scaling Group replaces them: you set the ASG health check type to ELB so the group terminates instances the ALB considers unhealthy and launches fresh ones. If the whole fleet is unhealthy, you scale out to add capacity and you check whether the health check path, port, and thresholds are correct — a health check hitting a path that returns 404, or with a timeout shorter than the app's startup time, marks healthy instances as failed. The longer-term fix is to make the health check accurate: point it at a lightweight readiness endpoint that returns 200 only when dependencies are ready, tune the healthy and unhealthy thresholds and grace period so slow-starting apps are not killed prematurely, and add startup-time dependency checks so a new instance does not go into service before its database and cache connections are warm.

For an RDS running out of storage, the immediate mitigation is to add storage now. Modern RDS supports storage autoscaling, so the fastest safe action is to raise the max allocated storage and let it grow, or manually increase the allocated storage, which RDS does online without downtime for most engines. You also free space fast by purging or archiving old data and by clearing bloat — for example rotating large logs or dropping stale temp tables. The longer-term fix targets the growth driver: enable storage autoscaling permanently with a sensible ceiling, set CloudWatch alarms on FreeStorageSpace well before exhaustion (for example at 20 percent free), move cold data to cheaper storage or an archive, implement data retention and partition pruning so old transactions roll off, and review whether an unindexed query or a runaway job is writing far more than expected.

For a failed production deployment, the immediate mitigation is to roll back to the last known-good version, because rollback is almost always the fastest safe way to restore service. With a blue-green setup you flip traffic back to the stable environment instantly; with a rolling deployment you redeploy the previous image or use your platform's rollback; with Kubernetes you run a rollout undo. You also flip off any new feature flag the release introduced. The longer-term fix closes the pipeline gap that let the bad build through: add or strengthen automated tests and a staging smoke test that mirrors production, add health gates and automatic rollback on error-rate or latency regression, use progressive delivery such as canary so a bad release only affects a small percentage before it is caught, and make deployments reversible by always keeping the previous version warm. A senior nuance across all three is that mitigation and root cause are different phases: you restore service first while communicating status, and you only begin deep root-cause analysis once the system is stable, because every minute of outage costs customers and money.
sections.s3_banking:
The National Bank of India platform hits three incidents: EC2 instances failing ALB health checks, an RDS nearing full storage, and a failed production deployment. We want one incident responder that, given the incident type, applies the correct immediate mitigation and records the longer-term fix.

Problem 1 — Each incident type needs a different, specific mitigation, and applying the wrong one wastes precious minutes. This is exactly what a strategy-per-incident design solves: pick the right mitigation handler at runtime.

Problem 2 — Mitigation must happen before root cause, and we must still capture the longer-term fix so it is not forgotten once service is restored. We model each handler as returning both the immediate action taken and the recommended permanent fix.

Problem 3 — We need a clear, logged audit of what was done, because in banking every production action is reviewed. Our runnable Java simulation models an `IncidentMitigator` interface with concrete handlers for EC2, RDS, and deployment incidents, selected by an `IncidentResponseEngine`. Classes: `Incident`, `MitigationResult`, `IncidentMitigator`, three handlers, `IncidentResponseEngine`, and an `IncidentResponseDemo` main.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build
mvn clean package -DskipTests

# Run the incident response demo
java -cp target/classes com.bank.incident.IncidentResponseDemo

# Real mitigation commands
aws autoscaling set-instance-health --instance-id i-0abc --health-status Unhealthy
aws rds modify-db-instance --db-instance-identifier bankingdb --allocated-storage 500 --apply-immediately
aws rds modify-db-instance --db-instance-identifier bankingdb --max-allocated-storage 1000
kubectl rollout undo deployment/transfer-service
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input: three incidents arrive — EC2 health failures, RDS storage near full, and a failed deployment.

Step 1 — The EC2 incident enters the engine. The engine finds `Ec2HealthMitigator` handles the type, which replaces unhealthy instances via the Auto Scaling Group set to ELB health checks and scales out for headroom, then records the long-term fix of a correct readiness endpoint and tuned thresholds.

Step 2 — The RDS incident enters. `RdsStorageMitigator` raises max storage and enables autoscaling online with no downtime and purges old audit logs to free space immediately, then records the permanent fix of autoscaling with a ceiling, an alarm at 20 percent free, and data retention.

Step 3 — The deployment incident enters. `DeploymentMitigator` rolls back to the last known-good version and disables the new feature flag, then records the permanent fix of a staging smoke test, canary releases with automatic rollback, and keeping the previous version warm.

Step 4 — Each response is logged with both the immediate action and the long-term fix, giving the on-call engineer a restore-now step and an audit trail of the permanent fix to schedule after service is stable.

Final output:

```
2026-10-30 02:08:00 [WARNING] INCIDENT: EC2_HEALTH — 6/8 banking-api instances failing ALB health checks
2026-10-30 02:08:00 [INFO   ]   MITIGATE NOW: Set ASG health-check type=ELB so unhealthy instances are terminated and replaced; scaled out +2 instances for headroom.
2026-10-30 02:08:00 [INFO   ]   LONG-TERM FIX: Point health check at /readiness (200 only when DB+cache ready), raise grace period above app startup time, tune healthy/unhealthy thresholds.
2026-10-30 02:08:00 [WARNING] INCIDENT: RDS_STORAGE — bankingdb RDS FreeStorageSpace at 3% — transactions failing to write
2026-10-30 02:08:00 [INFO   ]   MITIGATE NOW: Raised max allocated storage and enabled storage autoscaling (online, no downtime); purged 30-day-old audit logs to free space now.
2026-10-30 02:08:00 [INFO   ]   LONG-TERM FIX: Permanent storage autoscaling with ceiling; CloudWatch alarm at 20% FreeStorageSpace; data retention + partition pruning; archive cold transactions.
2026-10-30 02:08:00 [WARNING] INCIDENT: DEPLOYMENT — v4.2 transfer-service deploy spiking 5xx for Rajesh/Priya transfers
2026-10-30 02:08:00 [INFO   ]   MITIGATE NOW: Rolled back to last known-good version (kubectl rollout undo / flipped blue-green traffic to stable); disabled the new feature flag.
2026-10-30 02:08:00 [INFO   ]   LONG-TERM FIX: Add staging smoke test mirroring prod; canary release (5% first) with auto-rollback on error-rate/latency regression; keep previous version warm.
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
For any of these three incidents my approach is the same in structure: I separate immediate mitigation, which is the fastest safe action to restore service, from the longer-term fix that prevents recurrence, and I always mitigate first because every minute of outage costs customers and money. When EC2 instances fail ALB health checks, my immediate mitigation is to let the Auto Scaling Group replace them by setting its health-check type to ELB and scaling out for headroom, and my longer-term fix is to make the health check accurate by pointing it at a real readiness endpoint that returns 200 only when dependencies are ready and by tuning the grace period and thresholds so slow-starting instances are not killed prematurely.

When an RDS runs out of storage, my immediate mitigation is to grow storage now — raising the allocated storage online or enabling storage autoscaling, which most engines do without downtime — and to free space quickly by purging or archiving old data, and my longer-term fix is permanent storage autoscaling with a sensible ceiling, a CloudWatch alarm on free space at around 20 percent so I am warned long before exhaustion, and data retention with partition pruning so old transactions roll off automatically. When a production deployment fails, my immediate mitigation is to roll back to the last known-good version, because rollback is almost always the fastest safe restore — I flip blue-green traffic back or run a rollout undo and disable any new feature flag — and my longer-term fix is to close the pipeline gap with a staging smoke test that mirrors production and progressive canary delivery with automatic rollback on an error-rate or latency regression.

In my project at the National Bank of India this played out concretely: when banking-api instances failed health checks I replaced them through the ASG and then fixed the probe to hit a readiness endpoint; when the transactions database neared full I grew storage online and purged old audit logs, then made autoscaling and alarms permanent; and when a transfer-service release spiked 5xx errors for transfers involving Rajesh and Priya I rolled back immediately and then introduced canary releases with automatic rollback. The principle I always state to an interviewer is mitigate first and communicate status, keep deployments reversible and capacity elastic, and only begin deep root-cause analysis once the system is stable.
